Classifying Hypertension Risk in the African-American Community Using NHANES Data¶

Problem Statement¶

Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a critical public health concern in the United States, disproportionately affecting the African-American community. Studies show that African-Americans develop hypertension earlier and at higher rates than other racial groups, leading to increased risks of heart disease, stroke, and other complications.

The goal of this project is to build a classification model that predicts an individual's risk of hypertension based on lifestyle and socioeconomic factors using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). By identifying key predictors such as age, diet, physical activity, and healthcare access, this model can help improve early detection and preventive strategies.

Research Questions¶

This study aims to answer the following key questions:

  • What are the most important predictors of hypertension in the African-American community?
  • How well can a machine learning model classify individuals as hypertensive or non-hypertensive based on NHANES data?
  • Can insights from this model inform targeted health interventions to reduce hypertension risk?

Importance of the Study¶

Hypertension is a major contributor to health disparities in the U.S., particularly among African-Americans. If we can better understand the lifestyle and socioeconomic factors contributing to high blood pressure, we can develop more effective public health strategies and personalized interventions. However, ethical concerns such as data bias and misinterpretation of findings must be carefully considered to ensure responsible and fair use of predictive modeling in healthcare.

Data Source¶

The dataset used for this project comes from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which is publicly available through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). NHANES collects extensive health-related data through physical examinations, laboratory tests, and surveys.

  • CDC NHANES Data
  • NHANES on Kaggle

Dataset Overview¶

To build a classification model for hypertension risk, we will use the following NHANES datasets:

  1. Demographics Data (demographic.csv)

    • Includes participant age, gender, race, education, and income.
    • Key Variables:
      • RIDRETH1 → Race/Ethnicity (filtering for African-Americans)
      • RIDAGEYR → Age
      • RIAGENDR → Gender
      • DMDEDUC2 → Education level
      • INDHHIN2 → Household income

  2. Examination Data (examination.csv)

    • Contains direct measurements, including blood pressure readings.
    • Key Variables:
      • BPXSY1, BPXDI1 → First systolic & diastolic blood pressure reading
      • BPXSY2, BPXDI2 → Second systolic & diastolic reading
      • Hypertension Definition: Systolic BP ≥ 130 mmHg or Diastolic BP ≥ 80 mmHg

  3. Dietary Data (dietary.csv)

    • Provides information on nutrient intake.
    • Key Variables:
      • DR1TSODI → Sodium intake
      • DR1TKCAL → Total daily calories
      • DR1TPOTA → Potassium intake

  4. Physical Activity Data (physical_activity.csv)

    • Measures physical activity levels.
    • Key Variables:
      • PAQ605 → Days of moderate activity per week
      • PAQ620 → Days of vigorous activity per week

  5. Healthcare Access Data (questionnaire.csv)

    • Captures access to healthcare and general health perception.
    • Key Variables:
      • HIQ011 → Health insurance status (Yes/No)
      • HUQ030 → General health condition (Excellent/Poor)

Why This Dataset?¶

  • Comprehensive Data: NHANES offers detailed health and lifestyle factors crucial for predicting hypertension.
  • Real-world Relevance: The data is collected through nationally representative sampling, making it valuable for understanding public health trends.
  • Feature Availability: The dataset includes key risk factors such as age, diet, physical activity, and healthcare access, allowing us to explore their relationship with hypertension.

import pandas as pd


demographics = pd.read_csv(r"/Users/orlandobrandon/Desktop/Portfolio Files/orlandobrandon.github.io/Project_2/demographic.csv")
examination = pd.read_csv(r"/Users/orlandobrandon/Desktop/Portfolio Files/orlandobrandon.github.io/Project_2/examination.csv")
dietary = pd.read_csv(r"/Users/orlandobrandon/Desktop/Portfolio Files/orlandobrandon.github.io/Project_2/diet.csv")
questionnaire = pd.read_csv(r"/Users/orlandobrandon/Desktop/Portfolio Files/orlandobrandon.github.io/Project_2/questionnaire.csv")

# Filter for African-American participants
african_american_data = demographics[demographics["RIDRETH1"] == 4]  # 4 corresponds to African-Americans

# Merge datasets on 'SEQN'
merged_df = african_american_data.merge(examination, on="SEQN", how="inner")
merged_df = merged_df.merge(dietary, on="SEQN", how="inner")
merged_df = merged_df.merge(questionnaire, on="SEQN", how="inner")

# Handle missing values (drop rows with too many missing values)
merged_df = merged_df.dropna(subset=["BPXSY1", "BPXDI1", "DR1TSODI", "PAQ605", "HIQ011"])

# Define Hypertension Label (1 = Hypertensive, 0 = Non-Hypertensive)
merged_df["Hypertension"] = ((merged_df["BPXSY1"] >= 130) | (merged_df["BPXDI1"] >= 80)).astype(int)

# Class Distribution of Hypertension

            palette="viridis")
plt.xticks(ticks=[0, 1], labels=["Non-Hypertensive", "Hypertensive"])
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.title("Class Distribution of Hypertension")
plt.show()

# Age vs. Hypertension
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
sns.boxplot(x=merged_df["Hypertension"], y=merged_df["RIDAGEYR"], palette="coolwarm")
plt.xticks(ticks=[0, 1], labels=["Non-Hypertensive", "Hypertensive"])
plt.xlabel("Hypertension Status")
plt.ylabel("Age")
plt.title("Age Distribution by Hypertension Status")

from scipy.stats import ttest_ind, mannwhitneyu

# Split sodium intake by hypertension status
sodium_hypertensive = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 1]["DR1TSODI"]
sodium_non_hypertensive = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 0]["DR1TSODI"]

# Check normality using a histogram (optional)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.hist(sodium_hypertensive, bins=30, alpha=0.5, label="Hypertensive")
plt.hist(sodium_non_hypertensive, bins=30, alpha=0.5, label="Non-Hypertensive")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Sodium Intake Distribution")
plt.show()

# Perform T-test (assumes normality)
t_stat, p_value_ttest = ttest_ind(sodium_hypertensive, sodium_non_hypertensive, equal_var=False)

# Perform Mann-Whitney U test (for non-normal data)
u_stat, p_value_mannwhitney = mannwhitneyu(sodium_hypertensive, sodium_non_hypertensive)

# Display results
print(f"T-test: p-value = {p_value_ttest}")
print(f"Mann-Whitney U test: p-value = {p_value_mannwhitney}")

from scipy.stats import ttest_ind, mannwhitneyu

# Separate groups
mod_active_hyp = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 1]["PAQ605"]
mod_active_nonhyp = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 0]["PAQ605"]

vig_active_hyp = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 1]["PAQ620"]
vig_active_nonhyp = merged_df[merged_df["Hypertension"] == 0]["PAQ620"]

# T-test
t_test_mod = ttest_ind(mod_active_hyp, mod_active_nonhyp, equal_var=False, nan_policy="omit")
t_test_vig = ttest_ind(vig_active_hyp, vig_active_nonhyp, equal_var=False, nan_policy="omit")

# Mann-Whitney U Test (non-parametric)
mw_test_mod = mannwhitneyu(mod_active_hyp, mod_active_nonhyp, alternative="two-sided")
mw_test_vig = mannwhitneyu(vig_active_hyp, vig_active_nonhyp, alternative="two-sided")

# Print results
print(f"Moderate Activity - T-test p-value: {t_test_mod.pvalue}")
print(f"Moderate Activity - Mann-Whitney U test p-value: {mw_test_mod.pvalue}")

print(f"Vigorous Activity - T-test p-value: {t_test_vig.pvalue}")
print(f"Vigorous Activity - Mann-Whitney U test p-value: {mw_test_vig.pvalue}")

from numpy import mean, std
from math import sqrt

# Function to calculate Cohen's d effect size
def cohen_d(group1, group2):
    return (mean(group1) - mean(group2)) / sqrt((std(group1, ddof=1) ** 2 + std(group2, ddof=1) ** 2) / 2)

# Compute effect sizes for moderate and vigorous activity
effect_size_mod = cohen_d(mod_active_hyp.dropna(), mod_active_nonhyp.dropna())
effect_size_vig = cohen_d(vig_active_hyp.dropna(), vig_active_nonhyp.dropna())

# Print effect sizes
print(f"Effect Size (Cohen's d) - Moderate Activity: {effect_size_mod}")
print(f"Effect Size (Cohen's d) - Vigorous Activity: {effect_size_vig}")

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Compute Cramér's V
def cramers_v(chi2, n, k1, k2):
    return np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * min(k1 - 1, k2 - 1)))

n = len(merged_df)
k1 = len(merged_df["DMDEDUC2"].unique())
k2 = len(merged_df["Hypertension"].unique())

cramers_v_value = cramers_v(chi2_edu, n, k1, k2)
print(f"Cramér's V (Effect Size for Education & Hypertension) = {cramers_v_value}")

Reflections and Future Improvements¶

Challenges in Identifying Meaningful Predictors¶

One of the most significant challenges in this project was identifying features that had a meaningful correlation with hypertension. Initially, many of the features examined—such as physical activity levels and healthcare access—did not demonstrate a strong or statistically significant relationship with hypertension. This made feature selection a more complex process, requiring extensive statistical testing and visualization to find even weak trends.

Additionally, certain variables that seemed intuitively relevant (e.g., sodium intake, physical activity) had p-values that suggested no significant difference between hypertensive and non-hypertensive individuals. This highlights a key limitation of the dataset: while it contains valuable health-related variables, not all of them provide strong predictive power for hypertension classification.

Model Performance and Areas for Improvement¶

The final logistic regression model performed with an accuracy of approximately 61%, with a recall score on hypertensive cases that remained quite low. This suggests that while the model is decent at identifying non-hypertensive individuals, it struggles with correctly classifying those with hypertension. The relatively low precision and recall for the hypertensive class further indicate that the model is not capturing the most important risk factors effectively.

To improve the model in the future, I plan to:

  • Explore additional feature engineering techniques: Combining existing features or transforming variables (e.g., binning continuous variables into categories) might improve the model’s ability to differentiate between classes.
  • Incorporate external data sources: Bringing in more granular data on lifestyle factors, genetics, or environmental conditions could improve prediction accuracy.
  • Try different machine learning models: A decision tree-based approach, such as Random Forest or XGBoost, might capture non-linear relationships better than logistic regression.
  • Balance the dataset: Given the imbalance in hypertensive vs. non-hypertensive cases, applying oversampling (SMOTE) or cost-sensitive learning techniques could enhance model performance.

Key Takeaways¶

This project was an insightful exercise in feature selection, statistical analysis, and model evaluation. While finding meaningful predictors was more challenging than anticipated, the process reinforced the importance of rigorous testing and domain knowledge in data science. Moving forward, I will refine the model by integrating new approaches and further optimizing feature selection to improve classification accuracy.
